core.h: Absorption of mineral ions by active transport
core.p: Plants need mineral ions as well as water. The most important is **nitrate**, needed to make amino acids and therefore proteins. The soil solution is often **very dilute**, so the concentration of ions outside the root hair cell can be **lower** than inside. Simple diffusion would then move ions the wrong way, so the plant uses **active transport** to move ions **against the concentration gradient**, from dilute to concentrated.
bullets: Mineral ions are absorbed by **active transport** using **carrier proteins** in the cell surface membrane.
Active transport needs **energy from aerobic respiration** (ATP) in the mitochondria.
It moves ions **against the concentration gradient**: from lower to higher concentration.
**Nitrate ions** are absorbed for making **amino acids and proteins**.
**Magnesium ions** are absorbed for making **chlorophyll**.
Because energy is needed, active transport stops if the root is short of **oxygen** or is treated with a **respiratory inhibitor**.
Diffusion alone would only work if the soil were more concentrated than the cell, which is rare.
Active transport allows the plant to **accumulate** ions inside the cell to a higher concentration than the soil.
Water and mineral ions are taken up by **different processes** at the same surface: osmosis for water, active transport for ions.

callouts.p: Active transport is the movement of substances against a concentration gradient through a cell membrane, using energy from respiration.
Root hair cells have many **mitochondria** because active transport of mineral ions needs energy released by aerobic respiration.

core.h: Comparing osmosis, diffusion and active transport at the root hair
core.p: All three processes move substances across membranes, but they differ in direction, energy and the proteins involved. At the root hair surface, water arrives by **osmosis** and mineral ions arrive mainly by **active transport**. Examiners love a comparison table, and they want the words **partially permeable**, **concentration gradient** and **energy from respiration** used correctly.
bullets: **Diffusion**: net movement of particles down a concentration gradient; passive; no energy needed.
**Osmosis**: a special case of diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane, down a water potential gradient.
**Active transport**: movement against a gradient, using energy from respiration and carrier proteins.
All three involve the **cell surface membrane** as the partially permeable barrier.
Only active transport can move ions into the cell when the outside is more dilute.
The **cell wall** is not selective; the membrane is.
Rate of osmosis increases if the **water potential gradient** is steeper.
Rate of active transport is limited by the **number of carrier proteins** and by the **rate of respiration**.

callouts.p: A strong answer says: 'water enters by osmosis down a water potential gradient; mineral ions enter by active transport against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration'.

core.h: Why plants need water and mineral ions
core.p: Absorption is only useful if you can say what the substances are used for. Water is the raw material for **photosynthesis**, the solvent that carries dissolved substances, and it keeps cells **turgid** so the plant is supported. Mineral ions are needed in small amounts but are essential: **nitrate** for amino acids and proteins, **magnesium** for chlorophyll.
bullets: Water is a **reactant in photosynthesis** in the leaves.
Water keeps cells **turgid**, which supports the plant (herbaceous plants rely on this).
Water is the **solvent** in which mineral ions are transported and reactions occur.
**Nitrate ions** are used to make **amino acids**, which join to form **proteins** for growth and enzymes.
**Magnesium ions** are needed to make **chlorophyll**, which absorbs light for photosynthesis.
A plant short of nitrate shows **poor growth and yellowing (chlorosis) of older leaves**.
A plant short of magnesium shows **yellowing between the veins of older leaves (chlorosis)** because magnesium is moved to new growth.
Mineral ions are needed in **much smaller quantities** than water.
Root hair cells absorb both at the same time from the soil solution.

callouts.p: **Nitrate for proteins; magnesium for chlorophyll.** These two facts appear again and again.

core.h: How water moves on through the plant after absorption
core.p: Once water is inside the root hair cell it does not stay there. It moves across the root to the **xylem**, and from there it is carried up the plant. This links B2.2f to the transport section: the root hair is only the **entry point** of a continuous pathway. Water potential keeps falling as water is used and evaporated, so the gradient from soil to leaf is maintained.
bullets: Water crosses from cell to cell by osmosis, each time moving to a **lower water potential**.
Water reaches the **xylem** vessels in the centre of the root.
Xylem carries water **up** the plant from roots to leaves.
Water is **pulled** up the xylem as water evaporates from leaves (**transpiration**).
The continuous column of water is held together by **cohesion** between water molecules.
Mineral ions are also carried in the xylem in solution.
The whole pathway is soil to root hair to cortex to xylem to leaf.
The steeper the water potential gradient between soil and air, the faster water is absorbed.
Root hair cells replace the water they lose, so they stay turgid and functioning.

callouts.p: If a question asks why root hair cells matter to the whole plant, mention that they are the start of the transpiration stream to the xylem.

core.h: Required practical links and investigations involving root hair cells
core.p: OCR expects you to be able to plan and interpret investigations that show osmosis and active transport in plant tissue. The classic is **osmosis in potato cylinders** in different concentrations of sugar solution, and the classic active transport evidence is the effect of **respiratory inhibitors** or **low oxygen** on ion uptake. You must be able to state variables, control them, and calculate percentage change in mass.
bullets: **Osmosis in potato**: cut equal cylinders, blot dry, weigh, leave in a range of sugar concentrations, reweigh, calculate **percentage change in mass**.
Percentage change in mass = (final mass - initial mass) / initial mass x 100.
Potato gains mass in **pure water** (water enters by osmosis) and loses mass in **strong sugar solution**.
At the concentration where there is **no change in mass**, the water potential of the potato equals that of the solution.
**Control variables**: same potato, same size and surface area of cylinder, same time, same temperature.
**Repeat** and calculate a **mean** to improve reliability; identify anomalies.
Active transport evidence: root tissue in a **respiratory inhibitor** or in **low oxygen** takes up fewer mineral ions.
This shows ion uptake **needs energy from respiration**, unlike water uptake which continues.
Use a **water bath** to keep temperature constant, since temperature affects respiration rate.
Safety: wear eye protection with sugar solutions; use a tile when cutting.

callouts.p: Percentage change in mass = (final mass - initial mass) / initial mass x 100.
Cylinders must be **blotted dry** before each weighing, or surface water ruins the mass readings.

core.h: Common applied questions: fertilisers, waterlogging and salinity
core.p: Exam questions often give a farming context. Understanding osmosis and active transport lets you explain why **over-watering**, **salty soil** and **fertiliser** affect crops. The key idea is always the **water potential gradient** between soil water and cell sap, and the **oxygen supply** to the roots for respiration.
bullets: **Waterlogged soil**: air spaces fill with water, so **oxygen is scarce**, respiration slows, and **active transport of mineral ions falls**.
Waterlogging can also cause root death and wilting because damaged roots cannot absorb water.
**Salty soil**: the soil solution becomes **concentrated**, so its water potential falls below that of the cell sap.
Water then leaves the root hair cells by osmosis, the cells become **flaccid** and the plant **wilts**.
**Too much fertiliser** has the same effect as salty soil: it lowers the water potential of soil water.
**Nitrate fertiliser** increases protein synthesis and growth, but only if roots can respire to absorb it.
Farmers **drain** waterlogged fields to restore oxygen for respiration.
Plants adapted to salty soils have mechanisms to keep their cell sap concentrated.
The **net** movement of water always depends on the difference in water potential, not on the amount of water present.

head: Condition
Effect on soil water potential
Effect on plant
rows: Poor ion uptake, roots may die

callouts.p: For waterlogging, credit needs **both** 'less oxygen' and 'less energy for active transport of mineral ions'.

core.p: At Higher tier you must use **water potential** correctly, including the idea that solutes make water potential **more negative**, and that water moves by **net** movement. Triple science students should also be able to explain ion uptake in terms of **carrier proteins** and the **energy-requiring change of shape** of those proteins, and to link the process to the **mitochondria** and aerobic respiration in detail.
bullets: Adding solute **lowers (makes more negative) the water potential** of a solution.
Pure water has a water potential of **zero**; all solutions are negative.
Water moves from **less negative to more negative** water potential.
**Net movement** means the overall direction, even though water crosses both ways.
Active transport uses **carrier (transport) proteins** that combine with the ion and change shape to move it across.
The energy from respiration is used to **move the ion against its concentration gradient**.
Higher answers should name **ATP** as the energy source released by **aerobic respiration** in mitochondria.
If respiration is inhibited, carrier proteins cannot work and ion uptake stops.
Osmosis rate depends on the **steepness of the water potential gradient** and the **surface area** of the membrane.
Triple: root hair cells are adapted with **many mitochondria** precisely because of this energy demand.

callouts.p: Water potential is a measure of the tendency of water to move; pure water has a water potential of zero and adding solutes makes it more negative.
Writing 'soil water is -0.2 and cell sap is -0.8, so water moves into the cell' earns the gradient mark.

core.h: Exam command words and how to answer them
core.p: Most marks on this point come from **explain** and **describe** questions worth 2 to 4 marks, plus 6-mark extended answers that combine root hair adaptation with the two uptake processes. The trick is to name the process, state the direction using a gradient, and state whether energy is needed.
bullets: **Describe**: say what happens (water moves into the root hair cell).
**Explain**: give reasons using science (because the cell sap has a lower water potential).
**Compare**: use both processes and a linking word (whereas, while).
**Suggest**: apply the idea to a new context such as a waterlogged field.
**Calculate**: show the formula, substitution and answer with units.
For 6 marks, structure as: structure and surface area, osmosis, active transport, energy and mitochondria, uses of water and ions.
Always use **partially permeable**, **water potential**, **concentration gradient**, **active transport**, **respiration**.
Do not write 'the root hair sucks water in' or 'the cell absorbs water by diffusion'.

callouts.p: 'Water enters by osmosis from the soil (higher water potential) through the partially permeable membrane into the cell sap (lower water potential).' That is three marks in one sentence.

core.h: Quick recall check before the exam
core.p: Use this section as a final self-test. Cover the answers and say them out loud. If you can complete every line, you are at grade 9 standard for B2.2f.
bullets: Root hair cells are in the **root hair zone** behind the root tip.
The root hair gives a **large surface area** and a **short diffusion path**.
Water enters by **osmosis** down a **water potential gradient**.
The membrane is **partially permeable**; the wall is **freely permeable**.
Mineral ions enter by **active transport** against a **concentration gradient**.
Active transport needs **energy from respiration** and **carrier proteins**.
**Nitrate** makes amino acids and proteins; **magnesium** makes chlorophyll.
**Many mitochondria** are present for respiration.
Water then moves to the **xylem** and up the plant.
**Waterlogging** reduces oxygen, so ion uptake falls.
**Salty soil** lowers soil water potential, so water leaves the cell.
Percentage change in mass = (final - initial) / initial x 100.

callouts.p: Root hair cells absorb water by osmosis and mineral ions by active transport, because they have a large surface area, thin walls and many mitochondria.

analogy.t: The root hair cell is a long drinking straw with a one-way turnstile
analogy.p: Imagine the root hair as a very long, very thin **straw** pushed deep into a glass of soil water: the longer and thinner the straw, the more water touches it and the shorter the distance to your mouth, just as the root hair's length gives a large surface area and a short path. Water then behaves like people drifting **downhill** through a gate that only lets water through (the partially permeable membrane), moving from the crowded, dilute soil side to the more concentrated cell sap side. Mineral ions are like shoppers who need to go **uphill** into a shop: they cannot drift in, so they must pass through a **turnstile that needs a coin of energy** (the carrier protein powered by respiration), and if the power is cut off (low oxygen or a respiratory inhibitor) the turnstile stops and no ions get in. The analogy breaks down because a straw is passive and has no membrane at all, water molecules are not people and do not decide anything, and a real root hair is living, respiring and can rebuild itself, whereas a straw cannot.

terms.d: A plant epidermal cell of the root with a long extension that provides a large surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions.
The long, narrow extension of a root hair cell that projects into the soil.
A freely permeable wall made of cellulose that surrounds the cell and offers no barrier to water or dissolved ions.
A membrane that allows water molecules through but not most solute particles.
The net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane.
A measure of the tendency of water to move; pure water is zero and adding solute makes it more negative.
A difference in water potential between two regions that causes net movement of water.
The movement of substances against a concentration gradient through a cell membrane using energy from respiration.
A difference in concentration of a substance between two regions.
A membrane protein that binds a specific ion and changes shape to move it across the membrane during active transport.
The release of energy from glucose using oxygen, occurring in mitochondria and providing ATP for active transport.
Organelles where aerobic respiration takes place, abundant in root hair cells.
Mineral ions absorbed by roots and used to make amino acids and proteins.
Mineral ions absorbed by roots and used to make chlorophyll.
A cell that is swollen and firm because water has entered by osmosis and pushed the cytoplasm against the wall.
A cell that has lost water and is soft because the vacuole has shrunk.
Plant tissue that transports water and mineral ions from roots to leaves.
Water in the soil containing dissolved mineral ions, usually very dilute.

mistakes.w: The root hair cell absorbs water by diffusion.
mistakes.r: Water is absorbed by **osmosis** through a **partially permeable membrane**, down a water potential gradient.

mistakes.w: The root hair sucks water in / the cell drinks the water.
mistakes.r: Water moves by **net movement** down a **water potential gradient**; no sucking or active pulling by the cell occurs.

mistakes.w: Mineral ions diffuse into the root hair cell.
mistakes.r: Mineral ions are absorbed by **active transport** against a concentration gradient, using energy from respiration.

mistakes.w: The root hair cell wall is partially permeable.
mistakes.r: The **cell wall is freely permeable**; the **cell surface membrane** is partially permeable.

mistakes.w: Active transport needs no energy because it is fast.
mistakes.r: Active transport **requires energy (ATP) from aerobic respiration** and uses carrier proteins.

mistakes.w: Water enters because there is a high concentration of water outside.
mistakes.r: Use **water potential**: soil water has a **higher (less negative) water potential** than the cell sap.

mistakes.w: Root hair cells contain chloroplasts to make food.
mistakes.r: Root hair cells have **no chloroplasts** because they are underground with no light.

mistakes.w: Waterlogged soil damages roots because the soil water is too concentrated.
mistakes.r: Waterlogging means **too little oxygen**, so **respiration and active transport of mineral ions decrease**.

mistakes.w: A plant in salty soil wilts because it cannot absorb nitrate by diffusion.
mistakes.r: The soil solution has a **lower water potential** than the cell sap, so **water leaves the root hair cells by osmosis** and the plant wilts.

mistakes.w: Root hairs are the same as stomata or leaves.
mistakes.r: Root hairs are **extensions of root epidermal cells** in the root hair zone; stomata are pores in leaves.

exam.q: State two ways in which a root hair cell is adapted for the absorption of water and mineral ions.
model: It has a long extension that gives a large surface area for absorption.
It has a thin cell wall and membrane, giving a short diffusion distance / short path for water and ions.
exam.tip: Name the feature and immediately add the benefit; one mark each.

exam.q: Describe how water enters a root hair cell from the soil.
model: Water enters by osmosis.
Water moves from the soil (higher water potential) through the partially permeable cell surface membrane into the cell sap (lower water potential).
exam.tip: Always include the word osmosis and a water potential gradient.

exam.q: Explain why a root hair cell contains many mitochondria.
model: Mineral ions are absorbed by active transport.
Active transport needs energy released by aerobic respiration, which occurs in the mitochondria.
exam.tip: Link mitochondria to respiration to active transport in a chain.

exam.q: Explain why mineral ions are absorbed by active transport rather than by diffusion.
model: The concentration of mineral ions in the soil solution is often lower than inside the root hair cell.
Ions must move against the concentration gradient, which requires energy from respiration.
exam.tip: State the concentration comparison first, then the energy reason.

exam.q: A student placed potato cylinders in pure water and in a strong sugar solution. Explain the change in mass of the cylinder in pure water.
model: Water enters the potato cells by osmosis.
Water moves from the solution (higher water potential) into the cells (lower water potential), so the cylinder gains mass.
exam.tip: Describe direction and then link to mass change.

exam.q: Explain why the mineral ion content of a plant decreases when the soil is waterlogged.
model: Waterlogged soil has little oxygen / air spaces filled with water.
Roots cannot carry out aerobic respiration at the same rate.
Less energy (ATP) is released for active transport.
So fewer mineral ions are absorbed against the concentration gradient.
exam.tip: Four linked points; do not repeat 'no oxygen' in different words.

exam.q: A farmer grows crops in soil that has become very salty. Explain why the plants wilt.
model: The salty soil solution is more concentrated, so it has a lower (more negative) water potential than the cell sap.
Water therefore moves out of the root hair cells by osmosis.
The vacuole shrinks and the cells become flaccid.
The plant loses more water than it absorbs, so it wilts.
exam.tip: Compare the two water potentials explicitly to secure the first mark.

exam.q: Compare the absorption of water and mineral ions by a root hair cell.
model: Water is absorbed by osmosis; mineral ions by active transport.
Water moves down a water potential gradient; ions move against a concentration gradient.
Osmosis needs no energy; active transport uses energy from respiration.
Osmosis passes through the partially permeable membrane without carrier proteins; active transport uses carrier proteins.
exam.tip: Use 'whereas' or 'while' to show comparison rather than two separate lists.

exam.q: Explain how the structure of a root hair cell is related to its function. (6 marks)
model: Root hair cell is an epidermal cell with a long extension, giving a large surface area for absorption.
The thin cell wall and membrane give a short diffusion distance.
The cell wall is freely permeable so water passes through easily.
Water enters by osmosis down a water potential gradient through the partially permeable cell surface membrane into the concentrated cell sap.
Many mitochondria release energy by aerobic respiration.
This energy is used for active transport of mineral ions against the concentration gradient using carrier proteins.
Absorbed nitrate is used to make amino acids and proteins and magnesium to make chlorophyll.
exam.tip: Structure, osmosis, active transport, energy, uses: aim for one mark per distinct idea.

exam.q: Calculate the percentage change in mass of a potato cylinder whose initial mass was 4.0 g and final mass was 4.6 g.
model: Change in mass = 4.6 - 4.0 = 0.6 g.
Percentage change = 0.6 / 4.0 x 100 = 15 %.
exam.tip: Show the substitution; include the % sign.

exam.q: Suggest why a plant grown in soil lacking nitrate shows poor growth.
model: Nitrate ions are needed to make amino acids.
Amino acids are joined to make proteins needed for growth, so growth is poor.
exam.tip: Two-step chain: nitrate to amino acids to proteins.

exam.q: Explain why water uptake by a root hair cell continues even when a respiratory inhibitor is applied, but mineral ion uptake does not.
model: Water uptake by osmosis is passive and needs no energy from respiration.
Active transport of mineral ions needs energy from respiration, so it stops when respiration is inhibited.
exam.tip: Contrast passive and active in one sentence each.

worked.q: A potato cylinder has an initial mass of 5.0 g. After 30 minutes in pure water its mass is 5.4 g. Calculate the percentage change in mass and explain it.
steps: Change in mass = final mass - initial mass = 5.4 - 5.0 = 0.4 g.
Percentage change in mass = (change in mass / initial mass) x 100.
Substitute: (0.4 / 5.0) x 100.

Explain: pure water has a higher (less negative) water potential than the potato cell sap, so water enters the cells by osmosis through the partially permeable membrane, the vacuoles swell and the cylinder gains mass.
worked.ans: Percentage change in mass = +8 %. The cylinder gained mass because water moved into the potato cells by osmosis down the water potential gradient.

worked.q: A root hair cell has a cell sap water potential of -0.9 MPa. In dry soil the soil water potential is -1.2 MPa; after rain it is -0.3 MPa. Predict the direction of water movement in each case.
steps: Osmosis moves water from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential.
Dry soil: soil is -1.2 MPa and cell sap is -0.9 MPa, so the soil has the lower water potential.
Therefore water moves out of the root hair cell into the soil; the cell becomes flaccid and the plant wilts.
After rain: soil is -0.3 MPa and cell sap is -0.9 MPa, so the soil now has the higher water potential.
Therefore water moves into the root hair cell by osmosis; the cell becomes turgid.
worked.ans: In dry soil water leaves the root hair cell (net movement outwards, cell flaccid). After rain water enters the root hair cell by osmosis (cell turgid).

worked.q: A farmer drains a waterlogged field and applies a nitrate fertiliser. Explain, using active transport, why the crop's growth improves.
steps: In waterlogged soil the air spaces are filled with water, so oxygen concentration around the roots is low.
Low oxygen means less aerobic respiration in the mitochondria of root hair cells, so less ATP is released.
Active transport of nitrate ions against the concentration gradient therefore slows, so the plant absorbs little nitrate.
After drainage, oxygen returns, aerobic respiration increases and more ATP is available.
Carrier proteins in the cell surface membrane can now move more nitrate ions into the root hair cells.
Nitrate is used to make amino acids, which are joined into proteins for growth, so growth improves.
worked.ans: Drainage restores oxygen, so aerobic respiration and ATP supply rise, allowing active transport to absorb more nitrate ions; these are used to make amino acids and proteins, so the crop grows better.

bio_ocra.5.2.summary: The heart and blood vessels form a closed circulatory system that pumps blood round the body, delivering oxygen and nutrients while removing waste. The heart’s four chambers and associated valves ensure one‑way flow, and the arterial, capillary and venous networks are specialised for high‑pressure transport, exchange and low‑pressure return. Understanding their structure‑function relationships explains how size‑related challenges are overcome in humans.

core.p: The heart is a muscular organ located in the mediastinum, divided into right and left sides by the septum. Each side has an atrium (receives blood) and a ventricle (pumps blood).
bullets: Four chambers: right atrium (RA), right ventricle (RV), left atrium (LA), left ventricle (LV)
Interventricular septum separates ventricles; interatrial septum separates atria
Walls: atria have thin walls; ventricles have thick muscular walls (LV > RV) to generate higher pressure
Valves: atrioventricular (tricuspid on right, bicuspid/mitral on left) and semilunar (pulmonary, aortic) ensure unidirectional flow

callouts.p: A valve situated between an atrium and its corresponding ventricle that prevents back‑flow of blood.
The left ventricle generates the highest pressure in the circulatory system (≈120 mm Hg systolic).

core.p: Each chamber has a specific role in the double circulatory system, creating pressure gradients that drive blood flow.
bullets: RA receives de‑oxygenated blood from systemic veins → passes through tricuspid valve into RV.
RV pumps blood to the lungs via the pulmonary artery (pulmonary circulation).
LA receives oxygen‑rich blood from pulmonary veins → passes through bicuspid valve into LV.
LV pumps blood into the aorta for systemic distribution (systemic circulation).

callouts.p: Remember the sequence: RA → RV → lungs → LA → LV → body.

core.p: Arteries, veins and capillaries differ in wall thickness, lumen size and function, matching the demands of high‑pressure transport, exchange and low‑pressure return.
bullets: Arteries: thick tunica media (smooth muscle), elastic fibres, narrow lumen – withstand high pressure.
Arterioles: smallest arteries, major site of resistance and blood‑pressure regulation.
Capillaries: one‑cell‑thick endothelium, basement membrane only, lumen ~5‑10 µm – maximises surface area for exchange.
Venules: collect blood from capillaries, thin walls, larger lumen than capillaries.
Veins: thin tunica media, large lumen, valves prevent back‑flow, low pressure.

callouts.p: The middle layer of a blood vessel wall, composed mainly of smooth muscle and elastic fibres.

core.h: Blood flow direction – role of valves
core.p: Valves prevent back‑flow, ensuring blood moves in one direction through the heart and veins.
bullets: Atrioventricular valves (tricuspid, bicuspid) close when ventricles contract.
Semilunar valves (pulmonary, aortic) close when ventricles relax.
Vein valves are flap‑like structures that open towards the heart and close to stop gravity‑induced back‑flow.

callouts.p: Do not confuse the pulmonary artery (carries de‑oxygenated blood) with the pulmonary vein (carries oxygenated blood).

core.h: Pressure gradients and the cardiac cycle
core.p: Blood moves because of pressure differences generated during systole and diastole.
bullets: Systole: ventricles contract → pressure rises (LV ≈120 mm Hg, RV ≈25 mm Hg).
Diastole: ventricles relax → pressure falls, atria fill.
Pressure falls along the arterial tree; resistance mainly in arterioles.
Capillary hydrostatic pressure ≈15 mm Hg; oncotic pressure ≈25 mm Hg drives re‑absorption.

callouts.p: The larger pressure difference between LV and aorta drives systemic flow.

core.h: Adaptations for size – why a closed system is needed
core.p: A closed circulatory system overcomes the diffusion limits imposed by increasing body size.
bullets: Rapid transport of O₂, nutrients and waste over long distances.
High pressure generated by the heart maintains flow despite large vascular resistance.
Capillary networks provide a huge total surface area relative to volume, allowing efficient exchange.

callouts.p: Two separate circuits – pulmonary and systemic – that keep oxygenated and de‑oxygenated blood apart.

core.p: Capillaries are the site of material exchange; their thin walls and narrow lumen maximise diffusion rates.
bullets: Endothelium: single layer of squamous epithelial cells.
Basement membrane provides support but is permeable to small molecules.
Intercellular clefts (≈6 nm) allow plasma proteins to pass slowly.
Pericytes regulate capillary diameter and blood‑brain barrier integrity.

callouts.p: Capillary diameter ≈5‑10 µm, just large enough for red blood cells to pass in single file.

core.p: Blood is a specialised fluid whose components are adapted for efficient transport of gases, nutrients and waste.
bullets: Plasma (~55% of blood) – watery medium containing dissolved ions, glucose, hormones, proteins (albumin, globulins, fibrinogen).
Red blood cells (RBCs) – biconcave discs increase surface‑to‑volume ratio, contain haemoglobin for O₂ transport.
White blood cells – immune function (not directly part of this point).
Platelets – clotting (not directly part of this point).

callouts.p: A protein in red blood cells that binds up to four molecules of oxygen.

core.h: Practical: Measuring heart rate and pulse pressure
core.p: A typical OCR practical investigates how exercise influences heart rate and pulse pressure, linking structure to function.
bullets: Equipment: stopwatch, ruler, blood pressure cuff, pulse oximeter (optional).
Method: Record resting pulse, then have pupil jog for 2 min, record immediate post‑exercise pulse and blood pressure.
Observation: Heart rate and systolic pressure rise; diastolic pressure changes little.
Explanation: Exercise increases venous return → larger stroke volume → higher systolic pressure.

callouts.p: Use the same pupil for all trials to control for fitness level.

core.h: Clinical relevance – heart disease and vessel damage
core.p: Understanding normal structure helps explain how pathology disrupts function.
bullets: Atherosclerosis: plaque builds up in arterial intima, narrowing lumen, increasing resistance and blood pressure.
Valve stenosis (e.g., aortic stenosis) reduces opening area, raising upstream pressure and causing ventricular hypertrophy.
Heart failure: weakened ventricular walls cannot generate adequate pressure, leading to reduced cardiac output.

callouts.p: Do not state that veins carry oxygenated blood – only the pulmonary veins do.

analogy.t: The heart as a pump‑station and vessels as plumbing
analogy.p: Imagine a water treatment plant: the heart is the pump that creates pressure, large mains (arteries) carry water quickly to distant houses, narrow pipes (capillaries) spread the water over garden beds for absorption, and return pipes (veins) bring the used water back to the plant. The analogy breaks down because blood is a living fluid containing cells that can change shape, and vessels can actively contract (vasoconstriction), unlike rigid plumbing.

terms.d: Valve between an atrium and its ventricle that prevents back‑flow of blood.
Valve at the base of the pulmonary artery and aorta that prevents back‑flow into the ventricles.
Consists of tunica intima, thick tunica media (smooth muscle & elastic fibres), and tunica adventitia.
Movement of gases, nutrients and waste across the thin capillary wall by diffusion, filtration and osmosis.
Difference between systolic and diastolic blood pressure; reflects stroke volume and arterial compliance.
Volume of blood ejected by a ventricle in one contraction.
Heart rate × stroke volume; total volume of blood pumped per minute.
Large veins (superior and inferior) that return de‑oxygenated blood to the right atrium.
Largest artery; carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the systemic circuit.
Pathway carrying de‑oxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs and back to the left atrium.
Pathway carrying oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to body tissues and back to the right atrium.
Shape of red blood cells that increases surface‑to‑volume ratio for efficient gas exchange.

mistakes.w: The pulmonary artery carries oxygenated blood to the lungs.
mistakes.r: The pulmonary artery carries de‑oxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

mistakes.w: Veins have thicker walls than arteries because they carry more blood.
mistakes.r: Arteries have thicker walls to withstand higher pressure; veins have thinner walls and larger lumen.

mistakes.w: Capillaries have a muscular layer to control flow.
mistakes.r: Capillaries consist of only a single layer of endothelial cells; flow is regulated by arterioles.

mistakes.w: The left atrium pumps blood into the lungs.
mistakes.r: The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and passes it to the left ventricle.

mistakes.w: Blood pressure is the same throughout the circulatory system.
mistakes.r: Blood pressure falls from arteries to capillaries to veins due to resistance.

mistakes.w: All valves in the heart are the same type.
mistakes.r: The heart has two types of valves: atrioventricular (tricuspid, bicuspid) and semilunar (pulmonary, aortic).

mistakes.w: Heart rate is the only factor determining cardiac output.
mistakes.r: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume; both are important.

exam.q: Explain how the structure of the left ventricle enables it to generate the high pressure required for systemic circulation. (4 marks)
model: The left ventricle has a thick muscular wall (1) – more muscle fibres produce greater contractile force.
It has a small, conical shape that reduces the volume it must fill (2) – increasing pressure (P=F/A).
The aortic valve prevents back‑flow, ensuring pressure is maintained during systole (3).
Together these features allow a systolic pressure of about 120 mm Hg, sufficient to overcome systemic resistance (4).
exam.tip: Mention wall thickness, shape, and the role of the aortic valve.

exam.q: Compare the structure of arteries and veins and explain how these differences relate to their functions. (6 marks)
model: Arteries have a thick tunica media with elastic fibres (1) – allows them to withstand high pressure.
Arteries have a smaller lumen (2) – maintains pressure and speed of blood flow.
Veins have a thin tunica media (3) – less pressure to resist.
Veins have a larger lumen (4) – acts as a reservoir for blood.
Veins contain valves (5) – prevent back‑flow due to low pressure.
These structural differences enable arteries to transport blood quickly under high pressure and veins to return blood to the heart under low pressure.
exam.tip: Structure → function link for each vessel type.

exam.q: A pupil’s heart rate increases from 70 bpm at rest to 130 bpm after exercise. Explain how this change helps meet the increased demand for oxygen. (2 marks)
model: Increased heart rate raises cardiac output (heart rate × stroke volume), delivering more oxygen‑rich blood to tissues.
More frequent contractions also raise systolic pressure, speeding blood flow to active muscles.
exam.tip: Link heart rate → cardiac output → oxygen delivery.

exam.q: Describe the structure of a capillary and explain why this structure is ideal for exchange of gases and nutrients. (4 marks)
model: Capillary wall consists of a single layer of endothelial cells (1) – minimal diffusion distance.
Only a basement membrane (2) – thin but supportive, allowing easy passage of small molecules.
Lumen is very narrow (≈5‑10 µm) (3) – forces red blood cells to travel single file, maximising contact with the wall.
These features give a large surface‑area‑to‑volume ratio, facilitating rapid diffusion of O₂, CO₂, nutrients and waste (4).
exam.tip: Emphasise thin wall and large surface area.

exam.q: Explain why veins contain valves, giving two consequences if valves were absent. (4 marks)
model: Valves prevent back‑flow of blood as it returns to the heart against gravity (1).
Without valves, blood would pool in the lower limbs, causing swelling (2).
Pooling would reduce venous return, lowering cardiac output and blood pressure (3).
It could also increase the risk of varicose veins due to increased venous pressure (4).
exam.tip: Link valve function to gravity and circulation efficiency.

exam.q: State two adaptations of red blood cells that aid their function in transport. (2 marks)
model: Biconcave disc shape increases surface‑to‑volume ratio (1).
Contains haemoglobin which binds oxygen (2).
exam.tip: Give shape and haemoglobin.

exam.q: A diagram shows the heart with labelled chambers and valves. Identify the structure labelled ‘X’ and state its function. (2 marks)
model: X = Bicuspid (mitral) valve (1).
Prevents back‑flow of blood from the left ventricle into the left atrium during ventricular contraction (2).
exam.tip: Remember the four valves and their direction.

exam.q: Why does systolic blood pressure fall as blood moves from the aorta into the arterioles? (2 marks)
model: Arterioles have a much smaller lumen, creating high resistance (1).
According to the equation ΔP = QR, increased resistance causes a drop in pressure (2).
exam.tip: Use resistance concept.

exam.q: Outline a practical method to investigate the effect of exercise on pulse pressure. (4 marks)
model: Measure resting systolic and diastolic blood pressure with a cuff (1).
Have the pupil perform a 2‑minute jog (2).
Immediately re‑measure systolic and diastolic pressure (3).
Calculate pulse pressure (systolic – diastolic) before and after exercise and compare (4).
exam.tip: Include repeatability and safety.

worked.q: Calculate the cardiac output of a person whose heart rate is 75 bpm and stroke volume is 70 ml.
steps: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume
Convert stroke volume to litres: 70 ml = 0.07 L
75 bpm × 0.07 L = 5.25 L min⁻¹

worked.q: If the systolic pressure in the aorta is 120 mm Hg and the diastolic pressure in the veins is 8 mm Hg, what is the pulse pressure?
steps: Pulse pressure = systolic – diastolic
120 mm Hg – 8 mm Hg = 112 mm Hg

bio_ocra.5.5.summary: Transpiration, translocation, stomata, xylem and phloem are the key adaptations that allow plants to move water, minerals and sugars over large distances despite the constraints of surface‑area‑to‑volume ratio. Transpiration creates a negative pressure that pulls water up through the xylem, while phloem transports sugars from sources to sinks by a pressure‑flow mechanism. Stomata regulate gas exchange and water loss, linking the whole system to the environment.

core.p: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through stomata. It creates a water potential gradient that drives water up the xylem.
bullets: Occurs mainly from the mesophyll cells to the atmosphere
Requires a continuous water column in the xylem (cohesion‑tension theory)
Driving forces: **water potential gradient**, cohesion, adhesion, and tension

callouts.p: The process by which water is lost as vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, primarily through stomata.

core.p: Stomata are pores surrounded by a pair of guard cells that control their opening and closing, balancing CO₂ uptake for photosynthesis with water loss.
bullets: Guard cells are kidney‑shaped, contain chloroplasts, and are turgid when open
Opening is promoted by light (blue light), low internal CO₂, and high water availability
Closing is triggered by high internal CO₂, abscisic acid (ABA), and low water potential

callouts.p: Stomatal aperture directly influences the rate of transpiration and photosynthetic CO₂ uptake.

core.p: Xylem conducts water and dissolved mineral ions from roots to shoots. It consists of dead, lignified cells forming continuous tubes.
bullets: Main elements: tracheids and vessel elements (higher plants)
Lignified secondary walls give rigidity and prevent collapse under tension
Water moves upward by **cohesion‑tension** (negative pressure) generated by transpiration

callouts.p: A model explaining how water is pulled up the xylem as a continuous column due to cohesion between water molecules and tension created by transpiration.

core.p: Phloem transports organic nutrients, mainly sucrose, from source (e.g., mature leaves) to sink (e.g., roots, fruits). The pressure‑flow hypothesis describes the mechanism.
bullets: Living cells: sieve‑tube elements and companion cells
Sucrose is actively loaded into sieve tubes at the source → water follows osmotically → high turgor pressure
At the sink, sucrose is unloaded, water exits, lowering turgor pressure
Resulting pressure gradient drives bulk flow of sap

callouts.p: Any organ that produces more photosynthate than it uses (e.g., mature leaves).
Any organ that consumes or stores more photosynthate than it produces (e.g., roots, developing fruits).

core.h: Link between transpiration and xylem transport
core.p: Transpiration creates a negative water potential in the leaves, pulling water up the continuous xylem column from the roots.
bullets: Water potential (Ψ) hierarchy: Ψsoil > Ψroot > Ψxylem > Ψleaf > Ψair
Cohesion between water molecules prevents breakage of the column
Adhesion to the walls of xylem vessels helps maintain the column

callouts.p: When answering exam questions, always state the direction of water movement (soil → root → stem → leaf).

core.h: Link between phloem transport and source‑sink relationships
core.p: The pressure‑flow mechanism depends on active loading/unloading of sugars, creating a pressure gradient that drives flow.
bullets: Active loading uses H⁺‑ATPase to create an electrochemical gradient
Sucrose moves into sieve tubes via H⁺‑symporters
At the sink, sucrose is removed by diffusion into sink cells, reducing osmotic potential

callouts.p: Do not confuse xylem (upward, water only) with phloem (bidirectional, sugars + water).

core.p: Although not the main focus of this point, understanding the factors helps explain why stomatal regulation is vital.
bullets: Temperature – higher temperature increases kinetic energy of water molecules
Wind speed – removes saturated air layer, increasing gradient
Humidity – lower relative humidity raises water‑vapour pressure deficit
Light – opens stomata, increasing transpiration

core.p: A potometer measures the rate of water uptake, which is a proxy for transpiration rate under controlled conditions.
bullets: Set‑up: capillary tube, water reservoir, plant shoot, airtight joints
Measure displacement of water column over time
Control variables: light intensity, temperature, humidity

callouts.p: When describing the potometer, emphasise that it measures **water uptake**, not water loss directly.

core.h: Integration – how plants overcome size limitations
core.p: Small cells rely on diffusion, but large plants need specialised transport. Transpiration‑driven xylem and pressure‑flow phloem provide rapid, long‑distance movement of water and nutrients, while stomata regulate exchange with the atmosphere.
bullets: Surface‑area‑to‑volume ratio limits diffusion; transport tissues increase effective exchange area
Continuous water column in xylem bypasses the need for diffusion over metres
Phloem allows movement of non‑mobile sugars to growing parts

core.h: Higher‑tier / triple‑only extension – phloem loading mechanisms
core.p: Higher‑tier questions may ask you to compare active vs. passive loading and their ecological significance.
bullets: Active loading: energy‑dependent, creates high sucrose concentration, common in fast‑growing herbaceous plants
Passive loading: relies on diffusion through plasmodesmata, typical of many trees
Implication: active loaders can maintain higher pressure gradients, supporting rapid growth

callouts.p: Remember that **active loading** creates a larger osmotic potential difference, increasing phloem pressure.

analogy.t: Plant vascular system as a city’s water and delivery network
analogy.p: Imagine a city where water is pumped from a reservoir (roots) up tall skyscrapers (stems) through pressurised pipes (xylem). The pressure is created not by a pump at the top but by the city’s demand for water (transpiration) pulling it upward—just like people opening taps creates suction. Meanwhile, a fleet of delivery trucks (phloem) carries groceries (sugars) from a central supermarket (source leaf) to various neighbourhoods (sinks). The trucks move because the supermarket loads the trucks heavily (high pressure) and the neighbourhoods unload them (low pressure), creating a pressure gradient that drives the flow. The analogy breaks down because xylem transport is a continuous column of water under tension, not a series of pumps, and phloem flow can reverse direction depending on source‑sink changes, unlike one‑way delivery routes.

terms.d: Loss of water vapour from aerial plant parts, mainly through stomata.
Pores in the epidermis surrounded by a pair of guard cells that regulate gas exchange and water loss.
Kidney‑shaped epidermal cells containing chloroplasts; become turgid to open stomata.
Dead, lignified tissue (tracheids and vessels) that conducts water and mineral ions from roots to shoots.
Living tissue (sieve‑tube elements and companion cells) that transports organic nutrients, mainly sucrose, from source to sink.
Explanation of upward water movement in xylem driven by transpiration‑induced negative pressure, cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to vessel walls.
Organ that produces more photosynthate than it uses (e.g., mature leaf).
Organ that consumes or stores more photosynthate than it produces (e.g., root, fruit).
Model of phloem transport where active loading creates high turgor pressure at the source and unloading creates low pressure at the sink, driving bulk flow.
Energy‑dependent uptake of sucrose into sieve tubes, raising osmotic potential.
Diffusive entry of sucrose into sieve tubes via plasmodesmata, requiring no ATP.
Measure of the potential energy of water; water moves from higher (less negative) Ψ to lower (more negative) Ψ.
Apparatus that measures the rate of water uptake by a shoot, used as an indirect measure of transpiration rate.

mistakes.w: Transpiration is the same as evaporation from the soil
mistakes.r: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the plant’s aerial parts, not from the soil.

mistakes.w: Phloem transports water only
mistakes.r: Phloem transports sugars (mainly sucrose) together with water, but its primary role is nutrient transport.

mistakes.w: Xylem moves nutrients upward and sugars downward
mistakes.r: Xylem moves water and mineral ions upward only; sugars are moved by phloem.

mistakes.w: Stomata open when the plant is water‑stressed
mistakes.r: Stomata close in response to water stress (via ABA) to reduce water loss.

mistakes.w: Cohesion‑tension theory needs a pump at the roots
mistakes.r: The theory relies on tension generated by transpiration, not a root pump.

mistakes.w: All phloem loading is active
mistakes.r: There are both active and passive loading mechanisms; the type depends on plant species.

mistakes.w: Transpiration rate is independent of humidity
mistakes.r: Lower humidity increases the water‑vapour pressure deficit, raising transpiration rate.

mistakes.w: Potometer measures transpiration directly
mistakes.r: It measures water uptake, which is used as a proxy for transpiration under controlled conditions.

exam.q: Explain how transpiration creates a water potential gradient that drives water up the xylem.
model: Transpiration causes loss of water vapour from leaf mesophyll → reduces leaf water potential (Ψleaf becomes more negative).
Water moves from root (higher Ψ) to leaf (lower Ψ) to restore equilibrium.
Cohesion between water molecules keeps a continuous column; adhesion to vessel walls prevents collapse.
Resulting tension (negative pressure) pulls water upward through the xylem.
exam.tip: Start with definition of transpiration, then link to water potential and cohesion‑tension.

exam.q: Describe the structure of a stomatal complex and state two factors that cause stomata to close.
model: Stomatal complex = pore surrounded by two kidney‑shaped guard cells containing chloroplasts.
Stomata close in response to (i) high internal CO₂ concentration, (ii) low water potential (water stress) mediated by ABA.
exam.tip: Use the exact term ‘guard cells’ and mention ABA for water‑stress.

exam.q: Using the pressure‑flow hypothesis, explain how sugars are transported from a leaf (source) to a growing root (sink).
model: At the source leaf, sucrose is actively loaded into sieve‑tube elements via H⁺‑symporters, increasing osmotic potential.
Water follows osmotically, raising turgor pressure in the sieve tube.
At the sink root, sucrose is unloaded (active or passive), decreasing osmotic potential.
Water exits the phloem at the sink, lowering turgor pressure.
The resulting pressure gradient (high at source, low at sink) drives bulk flow of sap towards the root.
Thus sugars move from source to sink.
exam.tip: Mention both loading and unloading steps and the resulting pressure difference.

exam.q: State two differences between xylem and phloem.
model: Xylem consists of dead, lignified cells and transports water/minerals only upward; phloem consists of living sieve‑tube elements and companion cells and transports sugars (and water) in any direction.
Xylem transport is driven by transpiration‑induced tension; phloem transport is driven by a pressure gradient generated by active loading/unloading.
exam.tip: Use the terms ‘dead’ vs ‘living’ and ‘upward only’ vs ‘bidirectional’.

exam.q: A potometer shows that a plant takes up 0.12 ml of water in 5 min. Calculate the rate of water uptake in ml min⁻¹.
model: Rate = volume / time = 0.12 ml / 5 min = 0.024 ml min⁻¹.
exam.tip: Keep units consistent; answer to two significant figures.

exam.q: Why do plants in arid environments often have fewer stomata than plants in moist habitats?
model: Fewer stomata reduce the total stomatal pore area, limiting water loss by transpiration.
In arid conditions, conserving water is more critical than maximizing CO₂ uptake.
exam.tip: Link stomatal density directly to water‑loss control.

exam.q: Explain how active loading of sucrose into phloem creates a pressure gradient.
model: Active loading uses H⁺‑ATPase to pump H⁺ out of sieve‑tube cells, creating an electrochemical gradient.
Sucrose enters the sieve tube via H⁺‑symport, raising solute concentration.
Higher solute concentration lowers water potential, causing water to enter by osmosis.
Increased water entry raises turgor pressure at the source, establishing a pressure gradient.
exam.tip: Mention H⁺‑ATPase and osmotic entry of water.

exam.q: List three factors that increase the rate of transpiration.
model: Higher temperature, lower relative humidity, and increased wind speed (all increase the water‑vapour pressure gradient).
Increased light intensity (opens stomata).
exam.tip: Each factor should be a separate bullet.

exam.q: Compare active and passive phloem loading in terms of energy requirement and typical plant types.
model: Active loading requires ATP to transport sucrose into sieve tubes; typical of fast‑growing herbaceous plants.
Passive loading relies on diffusion through plasmodesmata; typical of many woody perennials.
Active loading creates a larger osmotic potential difference → higher pressure gradient.
Passive loading creates a smaller gradient, supporting slower transport.
exam.tip: Structure answer as a two‑column comparison if possible.

worked.q: A plant loses 0.30 g of water in 10 min during a transpiration experiment. What is the rate of transpiration in mg min⁻¹?
steps: Convert grams to milligrams: 0.30 g = 300 mg.
Rate = total loss / time = 300 mg / 10 min = 30 mg min⁻¹.

worked.q: If the sucrose concentration in a source leaf is 0.15 M and the phloem loading is active, explain why the turgor pressure at the source is higher than at the sink.
steps: Active loading uses ATP to concentrate sucrose in the sieve tube → raises solute concentration.
Higher solute concentration lowers water potential, causing water to enter by osmosis.
Increased water entry raises turgor pressure in the source sieve tube.
At the sink, sucrose is removed, water exits, lowering turgor pressure.
worked.ans: The active loading creates a higher solute concentration and thus a higher osmotic potential at the source, drawing water in and raising turgor pressure relative to the sink.
